nameStory: This little ground spider gets its scientific name from Tennessee, where it was first discovered and described by scientists. Like many spiders that don't have established common names, it's often just called by its scientific name, Sergiolus tennesseensis, which rolls off the tongue once you get used to it!
description: Sergiolus tennesseensis is a small, unassuming member of the stealthy ground spider family that quietly hunts prey on the forest floor. These spiders are typically small and darkly colored, helping them blend into leaf litter and soil. Like other ground spiders, they don't build webs to catch prey but instead actively hunt at night. They're quite rare in New England, with only a handful of confirmed sightings.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No hunting web at all - these spiders are active hunters that chase down their prey on foot, though they may create small silk retreats under rocks or logs

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, robust build typical of ground spiders, with a relatively flat profile that helps them squeeze under bark and stones

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider, easily overlooked among leaf litter - you'll need to look closely to spot these tiny hunters

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Most active at night when they emerge to hunt; during the day they hide under rocks, logs, or in leaf litter where they feel dry and cool to the touch

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally dark coloration that helps with camouflage against soil and decomposing leaves

habitat: Look for this elusive spider in deciduous and mixed forests where there's plenty of leaf litter and fallen logs to provide hiding spots. They prefer areas with loose, well-drained soil where they can easily move between hiding places. In New England, they're most likely found in mature woodlands with rich understory vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots to hunt and eventually mate.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be spotted during nighttime searches with a flashlight.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek more permanent shelter as temperatures drop and prey becomes scarcer.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, rocks, or in soil crevices, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being incredibly rare in New England with only 4 recorded observations, this spider has somehow managed to spread far from its Tennessee homeland - showing that sometimes the quietest, most unassuming creatures are the best at long-distance travel!
confusionNotes: With so few sightings, this spider could easily be confused with other small, dark ground spiders in the same family. The key is often location and careful examination by an expert, as many ground spiders look remarkably similar to the untrained eye.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England means that any potential sighting should be photographed and reported to local naturalist groups or universities, as each observation helps scientists understand how this species is expanding its range northward.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like the more common Variegated Ground Spider, S. tennesseensis appears to be much rarer in our region and may have slightly different habitat preferences. The Common Patterned Ant-mimic Ground Spider has more distinctive markings and, as its name suggests, mimics ants in its appearance and movement patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Sergiolus relatives, the Variegated Ground Spider is distinguished by its particularly mottled, bark-like camouflage pattern.

Among its Sergiolus relatives, this species is distinguished by having just one pale spot rather than the multiple spots or complex patterns seen in the Variegated Ground Spider or Common Patterned Ant-mimic Ground Spider.
Sergiolus minutus is distinguished from its relatives like the Variegated Ground Spider by its much smaller size and uniform dark coloration.
